description: We are STEM students from Egypt with a passion for science, technology, and space. We believe that innovation begins with curiosity, collaboration, and the willingness to explore new ideas. Our different skills, perspectives, and experiences enable us to creatively tackle challenges, learn from one another, and create solutions that can make a difference. By taking part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we can apply our curiosity and push ourselves to create solutions to real-world problems.
summary: NASA’s Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV) and Curiosity rover represent two different stories of space exploration. The LRV helped Apollo astronauts explore the Moon before being left behind after its missions. Curiosity landed on Mars in 2012 and continues searching for evidence of ancient habitable environments. Through their journeys and different destinies, MISSION: AFTERLIFE celebrates the legacy of NASA’s exploration machines and reminds us that even when a mission ends, its discoveries live on.
details:
“The Rover That Stayed” is a story, presented as a slide deck and an interactive website, told in the voice of NASA’s Apollo 16 Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV). The rover wakes up in the silence of the Descartes Highlands and remembers who built it (Boeing and General Motors, in just seventeen months), who sent it (NASA), and what it did: unfolding in about seven minutes, then carrying astronauts John Young and Charles Duke 26.7 kilometers across the highlands in April 1972, before being left behind, one of three rovers still on the Moon. A short comparison with Curiosity, still active on Mars after more than fourteen years, shows the difference between a machine that was left behind and one that is still working.

It turns what many people call “space junk” into a human story, so students and general audiences can see discarded equipment as part of exploration history. The language is simple enough for younger learners, and every fact can be traced to NASA sources.

We want people to stop seeing abandoned equipment as leftovers and start seeing it as a record of what humans achieved. If the audience remembers the rover, learns its real numbers, and asks what should happen to machines when their missions end, the project has done its job.

We built the slide deck with [name of slide tool] and the interactive website . We used AI tools [add names] for research and for drafting the story text. All figures come from NASA documents, and NASA photographs are credited to NASA.

Instead of listing facts, we let the rover tell its own story as it remembers its journey, which gives a machine a voice and lets the audience feel what “abandoned” means. The drama is built on real data: mission numbers, dates, and engineering details from NASA documents.

Accuracy: we used NASA documents for every figure and kept dramatic lines separate from facts. Audience: we kept the language simple and the opening friendly for younger readers. Honesty: Curiosity is still an active mission, so we present it as a contrast, not as abandoned equipment.
